Nestlings of the Copper sunbird (Cinnyris cupreus) emerge from eggs weighing just 1.09 grams [Ww0 = 1.09 grams] at hatching, which is a remarkably low initial mass even for a small nectarivore, reflecting the extreme altricial state of passerine neonates. The incubation period lasts approximately 14 days [ab = approximately 14 days] when eggs are maintained at a constant 34 °C [T = 34 °C], a duration that is typical for birds of this body size and consistent with the thermal regime experienced in natural nest cavities across much of the species' sub-Saharan range. Upon hatching, the naked, blind young are entirely dependent on biparental provisioning, and their rapid early growth is fuelled by a steady intake of small arthropods and nectar delivered by both parents. The minimal hatchling mass imposes a substantial energetic burden on the breeding pair, as the chicks must more than sextuple their body weight before reaching fledging age.

Field studies indicate that under typical ambient conditions, the time from hatching to fledging is approximately 16 days [tx = approximately 16 days] when brood temperatures average 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], a value that aligns well with the rapid developmental schedules observed in other small African sunbirds. During this late nestling phase, pin-feathered chicks begin to thermoregulate independently and rapidly accumulate flight feather mass. Their departure from the nest at this age is a critical transition, as young birds must then learn to locate floral resources and avoid aerial predators while still being fed occasionally by parents. The fledging age of 16 days appears to represent a compromise between the need to minimize time spent in a vulnerable nest and the requirement to achieve adequate flight muscle development. Mortality rates are high immediately following nest departure, with many first-year individuals failing to survive the post-fledging period of low foraging efficiency.

Sexual maturity in this species is attained relatively quickly compared to other nectarivorous passerines, with puberty occurring at 48 days after hatching [tp = 48 days after hatching] under the same thermal conditions of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This rapid maturation is likely an adaptive response to the seasonal availability of nectar resources, allowing individuals born early in the breeding season to breed themselves before the flowering peak subsides. Young males begin to display adult iridescent plumage shortly after reaching puberty and start to establish feeding territories, while females develop the physiological capacity for clutch production. The early onset of reproductive capability also increases the potential for multiple overlapping generations within a single breeding season.

First reproduction, however, is typically deferred until approximately 365 days after hatching [tR = approximately 365 days after hatching] when held at 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], a delay that reflects the time required to acquire sufficient body condition and territorial resources for successful nesting. This first breeding event usually coincides with the onset of the rainy season in the species' savanna and woodland habitats. Females construct a small, domed nest in which they lay between 1 and 3 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 1 and 3 eggs per clutch], producing approximately 2 clutches per year [F_R_i = approximately 2 clutches per year], a reproductive output that balances the high energetic cost of parental care with the necessity of maintaining adult condition throughout the year. The brood size varies with food availability, and larger clutches are typically associated with periods of peak nectar abundance.

Adult females ultimately reach a body mass of about 8.1 grams [Wwi = about 8.1 grams], while adult males attain a slightly greater ultimate wet weight of 9 grams [Wwi = 9 grams], a modest sexual size dimorphism that is common among sunbirds and likely related to male-male competition for floral territories. In terms of metabolic physiology, respirometry trials conducted under thermo-neutral conditions have measured a basal metabolic rate of 29.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 29.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour] at a body temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], a rate that is broadly consistent with the energetic demands of a bird of this size. Maximum lifespan in the wild is estimated at approximately 11.9 years [am = approximately 11.9 years] under the same thermal regime of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], although few individuals likely reach this upper bound given the high predation pressure typical of African savanna ecosystems.
